items.title: Former Porn Star Reveals Key to Unlocking Shame, Embracing Freedom
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "Shame is not God's intention for your life."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

If anyone knows the grip of shame, it’s a former porn star.

Joshua Broome spent years in the pornography industry before finding faith in God, abandoning a life driven by sexual sin and drug abuse, and becoming a husband and father to four boys.

Since his salvation 11 years ago, Broome has become an outspoken evangelist and advocate against the dangers of pornography. One of the barriers to healing, he explained to CBN News, is shame.

“Shame is not God’s intention for your life,” he said. “The solution to shame is connection, is confession.”

Before he learned the Gospel, Broome said it was shame — rather than enjoyment— that kept him trapped in the pornography industry for years. He explained that, while guilt reveals, “I’ve done something wrong,” shame wrongly convinces a person, “I am someone wrong.”

“If I believe that my only value is indicative of me selling myself for sex, well, then, of course I’m going to continue doing what I’ve done, because it’s just an overflow of who I am,” he said.

From the Old to the New Testament, the Bible is clear about the need for confession for spiritual healing.

In Proverbs 28:13, King Solomon wrote, “People who conceal their sins will not prosper, but if they confess and turn from them, they will receive mercy” (NLT).

Then, in 1 John 1:8-9, it’s written, “If we claim we have no sin, we are only fooling ourselves and not living in the truth. But if we confess our sins to him, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleans us from all wickedness” (NLT).

And in James 5:16, James wrote, “Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The earnest prayer of a righteous person has great power and produces wonderful results” (NLT).

The key to breaking the cycle of shame, Broome emphasized, is honest and complete confession.

“The depth of your confession is going to equate to the level of your healing,” he said. “So say all of it.”

He continued, “The way that you own your past is you have to own it, and the way that you own it is you say it out loud because we can only be as free as we’re willing to be honest.”

For many, Broome said, the root of pornography use is not lust or even sex; more often than not, it’s tied to something much deeper: insecurity, loneliness, an unhealthy understanding of intimacy.

The truth is conversations about past sins or sin struggles are not easy. Broome and his wife, Hope, have had their fair share of difficult conversations over his sexual history. But the truth is, while accountability and responsibility are essential to spiritual growth, confession should be met with compassion.

“[My wife] looked at me and said, ‘Hey, I don’t want to minimize your pain … but I do want to tell you that you’re not defined by the worst thing you’ve ever done, and you won’t be defined by the greatest thing you ever do, because you’re not the author of you — God is,'” Broome recalled. “At the cross, the worst of us meets the best of God, and He wins. That’s how you defeat shame.”

Broome and his wife are the hosts of a new six-part series from XO Marriage, “Made Whole: Healing, Wholeness, and Holiness in a Sex-Saturated World.” You can access the course for free here.

Watch our wide-ranging conversation with Broome in the video above.

items.title: Celebrity Wishes for Perez Hilton’s Recovery — Then Takes It Back: Why?
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Perez Hilton’s livestream was the stuff of nightmares — a potentially demonic episode — and has laid bare the dark underbelly of social media, in more ways than one.

On the periphery of the scandal, a TikTok live video feed that ran nearly half an hour and showed Hilton covered in blood and repeatedly harming himself, was another troubling indication of cultural decay: a society that cares not about praying for our enemies but about getting even.

Jared Padalecki, who rose to fame in the early 2000s as one of the stars of “Gilmore Girls,” has used his clout to advocate for mental wellness, so it’s particularly striking to see him not only rescind but apologize for wishing Hilton well amidst his recovery from what was and will be a decisively defining and deeply dark moment in his life.

Initially, Padalecki wrote on social media, “I hope you are trying as best as you can to be kind to yourself right now. Please surround yourself with the love and support that all humans deserve.”

It wasn’t long before the “Supernatural” star faced swift condemnation for his kindhearted message to the celebrity gossip blogger. Padalecki deleted the post and apologized for publicly hoping for healing for Hilton, telling critics he “didn’t know” about the columnist’s career.

Padalecki went on to apologize for his “words caus[ing] any harm” and added he hopes everyone is “taking care of yourselves.”

It was Padalecki’s first instinct — his wish for Hilton’s healing — that was correct, regardless of Hilton’s checkered past and his indefensible work as a gossip blogger, actions that undoubtedly caused harm to the celebrities who were subject to his coverage.

That’s exactly what Jesus commands of us as His followers in Matthew 5:44-47 (NLT).

“But I say to you,” Jesus preached, “love your enemies! Pray for those who persecute you! In that way, you will be acting as true children of your Father in heaven.”

He went on to say, “For He gives His sunlight to both the evil and the good, and He sends rain on the just and the unjust alike. If you love only those who love you, what reward is there for that? Even corrupt tax collectors do that much. If you are kind only to your friends, how are you different from anyone else? Even pagans do that.”

Then, in Romans 12:17-21 (NLT), the Apostle Paul warned against taking revenge or seeking vengeance against others:

Never pay back evil with more evil. Do things in such a way that everyone can see you are honorable. Do all that you can to live in peace with everyone. Dear friends, never take revenge. Leave that to the righteous anger of God. For the Scriptures say, ‘I will take revenge; I will pay them back,’ says the Lord.

Instead, ‘If your enemies are hungry, feed them. If they are thirsty, give them something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals of shame on their heads.’

Don’t let evil conquer you, but conquer evil by doing good.

Our petition for God to intervene for the healing of another human being made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27) should never be predicated on what he or she has done in the past. Rather, it should be evidence of an outpouring of gratitude for a forgiveness gifted to us by a Savior who asks each of us to forgive one another in the same way God, through Jesus, has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:32).

Hilton, who in recent months has professed a faith in Jesus, needs prayer — regardless of the sins of his past.

All of us should absolutely be held accountable for our errors, missteps, and wrongdoings; taking responsibility for our actions is a necessary consequence of the choices we each make in this life. None of that, though, absolves us of the duty to pray for those around us or to need the prayers of others.

In the King James Version translation of 1 Peter 2:9, the Apostle Peter wrote that believers are “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people” in the world.

While social media is preying on our worst instincts — our fallen nature — to belittle, disparage, and denigrate, we follow a God who is calling us to do the opposite, to be peculiar by praying for the redemption of those trapped in dark places distant from the Lord.

As the psalmist wrote, I pray that, even as Hilton walks through the “darkest valley,” he would find the Shepherd who “leads me beside peaceful streams,” “renews my strength,” and “guides me along right paths” (Psalm 23:1-4, NLT).

items.title: Precious Parting Words
items.author: Nancy Gavilanes
items.summary: My friend José was in hospice care, dying. He’d been alert and talkative during my prior visit but a week later was now frail and speechless. I sat with José and his family anyway, hoping my presence would mean something to them. At the end of what would be my final visit, I was
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

My friend José was in hospice care, dying. He’d been alert and talkative during my prior visit but a week later was now frail and speechless. I sat with José and his family anyway, hoping my presence would mean something to them. At the end of what would be my final visit, I was the last one in the room with him. I finally stood and slowly headed to the door but stopped and turned around one last time to say, “Love you,” not expecting a response. There I saw José moving his lips. He was mouthing the words “love you” in return.

A person’s parting words can leave a lasting impression. As Jesus was getting ready to return to His Father in heaven after His sacrificial death and resurrection, He assured His disciples that all authority on heaven and earth belonged to Him (Matthew 28:18). And He left them with this lasting charge or Great Commission, “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you” (vv. 19-20). Christ also assured His followers that He would always be with them (v. 20).

Jesus’ parting words are for us today, too. May we embrace His call to tell others about Him so they can experience His love and forgiveness, live for Him, and enjoy eternal life with Him in heaven. His message is too good not to share with people of all nations.

items.title: What My Rental Car Taught Me
items.author: Adam Holz
items.summary: I recently traveled to Los Angeles and had to rent a car. Soon, I was driving through narrow downtown lanes, full of traffic and people. I found myself driving very carefully, slower than normal. Why? Well, I didn’t want to have an accident. But I really didn’t want to damage my rental c
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

I recently traveled to Los Angeles and had to rent a car. Soon, I was driving through narrow downtown lanes, full of traffic and people. I found myself driving very carefully, slower than normal. Why? Well, I didn’t want to have an accident. But I really didn’t want to damage my rental car. It wasn’t mine, after all. I was just, well, borrowing it.

Most of the time, we’d rather be owners than renters. But, as I drove, I couldn’t help but think that renting that car illustrated something important about my relationship to God.

Scripture teaches that even our bodies—which we might think we own—don’t belong to us. In a larger conversation about sexual sin in 1 Corinthians 6, Paul concludes, “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honor God with your bodies” (vv. 19-20).

I’ll admit, it’s hard to completely comprehend that my body is not my own. Still, God calls us to honor Him with it. To care for our bodies. To realize that we are stewards—renters, if you will—of these vessels He’s given us, that we might use them to honor and serve the One whose own broken body and blood saved us.

items.title: The White Sox Handed Out 40,000 Pope Hats and It Became the Biggest Giveaway in Team History
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: The White Sox were expecting a fun promotion Tuesday night. They ended up making franchise history. What started as a giveaway for 2,500 fans ballooned into a ballpark-wide celebration after demand for the team’s Pope Leo XIV-themed hats far exceeded expectations. By first pitch at Rate Field, more
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

The White Sox were expecting a fun promotion Tuesday night. They ended up making franchise history.

What started as a giveaway for 2,500 fans ballooned into a ballpark-wide celebration after demand for the team’s Pope Leo XIV-themed hats far exceeded expectations. By first pitch at Rate Field, more than 40,000 white papal-style hats featuring the White Sox logo had been handed out — the largest promotional giveaway in franchise history.

The reason? Chicago wanted to celebrate one of its own.

Long before he became Pope Leo XIV, Robert Prevost was a kid growing up in the working-class suburb of Dolton on Chicago’s South Side. He’s been open about his lifelong White Sox fandom, and ever since becoming the first American pope, the team has embraced him as perhaps its most famous fan.

The promotion quickly took on a life of its own. Originally limited to fans who purchased a special ticket package, the White Sox announced in July that the giveaway would be expanded to everyone attending the Aug. 11 game after interest exploded online. By Tuesday night, nearly 41,000 fans had packed the stadium, many arriving early to make sure they got one of the now-iconic hats.

The White Sox leaned into the moment throughout the game. During the fifth inning, the videoboard displayed “Peace be with you,” prompting a stadium-wide response from fans who happily played along. The visual was exactly as delightful as it sounds: tens of thousands of fans wearing oversized white pope hats with the Sox script logo while cheering on their hometown team.

5th Inning ‘Peace Be With You’ was a movie pic.twitter.com/zuOq4tC5jB

— Brett Haffner (@haffball7) August 12, 2026

The timing hasn’t hurt, either. After three straight disappointing seasons, the White Sox have become one of baseball’s surprise stories this year. Tuesday’s crowd watched a team that’s back above .500 and firmly in the playoff conversation, giving South Side fans another reason to celebrate.

For one night, though, the standings almost felt secondary.

The promotion wasn’t really about Catholicism as much as it was about hometown pride. Pope Leo isn’t just the leader of the Catholic Church to Chicagoans — he’s also the kid from Dolton who never stopped rooting for the Sox. Tuesday’s record-setting turnout showed just how much that connection still means.

Not every team gets to claim the pope as a lifelong fan. The White Sox decided to lean into it, and more than 40,000 people happily put on the hat.

items.title: ‘I Saw Myself Translated’: Language, Education, and the Love of Latin
items.author: Daniel Fitzpatrick
items.summary:
Daniel Fitzpatrick

By learning faithfully to use our words, by tuning them to the highest pitch we can manage, we advance toward harmony with the Word himself.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Daniel Fitzpatrick

If the final purpose of education is to lead the human person out of the bondage of ignorance and sin into the illumination of intellect and freedom of will found in communion with the triune God, then the educational journey must be one conducted along the pathways of the Logos. Following the Word, we encounter and come to know most deeply both the things made through the Word and the words whereby we cultivate and express our knowledge. And, in the process, we hope that we ourselves will be written into the story of salvation. 

En route, we deal with the business of language, this strange human gift that both unifies us and sets us at dis-ease. “It is impossible to say just what I mean!” cries Prufrock. Still, by some alchemy, the stuff of thought becomes on the page or in the air a means of communion, of recognition. “That’s how it is!” we say in the face of the perfect poem. In words, we give ourselves. We find ourselves. And we find, too, in earliest childhood or in the schoolroom, that language is a tricky thing, fraught with rules and customs and the other trappings of community. 

Nonetheless, the student who gives himself to the study of words and their rules often meets with delight, with a sense that the structure of words somehow traces the structure of the world. Where education is concerned, I submit not only that cultivation of such linguistic delight—and insight—is at the heart of the work of being led out into communion with the Word, but also that Catholic educators can best serve their students by training them not only in their native tongues but in foreign ones as well, and that pride of place still belongs to Latin.

Language as Triangulation

Readers of Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick have long noted an oddity of the book’s beginning, the so-called land chapters: They feature a surprising amount of doubles. Ishmael visits two port cities: New Bedford and Nantucket. He stays in two inns: The Spouter and the Try-pots. He goes to a black church and a white church. He meets the two owners of the Pequod. He enjoys two types of chowder. While some have supposed that Melville was simply getting his bearings, it seems more to the purpose that he was in fact giving us ours. By giving us two points whereby we might navigate, Melville allows us to triangulate our own position with respect to the text.

Indeed, language itself is a triangular matter. St. Augustine, standing near the headwaters of the stream of semiotics, drew distinctions among the sounds of words, their meanings, and the things they signify. The word “deer” on the page differs from the concept of deer, whose concept is itself a different thing still from the many individual creatures in the world that answer to the name of deer. And indeed, this triadic nature of our human power of language is critical to an understanding of how language carves along the joints of reality. 

The study of languages is thus critical to the reinvigoration of education precisely inasmuch as it helps students to better appreciate their own being with respect to signs and to things, and the study of foreign languages performs this function both by giving students more conceptual points of contact with reality and by bringing to life the capacities of language in itself. 

In an especially popular passage in his Surprised by Joy, C. S. Lewis describes his tutelage in Greek under a man known as “The Great Knock.” Sailing into Homer, Lewis finds himself becoming more and more fluent in the language until he finds that it is becoming conceptually transparent to him. As he puts it, 

I was beginning to think in Greek. That is the great Rubicon to cross in learning any language. Those in whom the Greek word lives only while they are hunting for it in the lexicon, and who then substitute the English word for it, are not reading the Greek at all; they are only solving a puzzle. The very formula, ‘Naus means a ship,’ is wrong. Naus and ship both mean a thing, they do not mean one another. Behind Naus, as behind navis or naca, we want to have a picture of a dark, slender mass with sail or oars, climbing the ridges, with no officious English word intruding.

Learning another tongue both increases a student’s facility with words and demonstrates to a student the gap that exists between words themselves and the things they signify. While Lewis is here remarking on the experience as it came to him through Greek, it is to be supposed that many a student will enjoy a similar process: In reading many times the Latin word “Danaos,” he will come not simply to think to himself “the Greeks” but to see in his mind a warrior band encamped around fires down on the beach or lying concealed within the hull of the great horse or gathered around a cold slab where a kingly father has prepared his daughter for sacrifice in the service of war. 

At the same time, language study often opens students to formerly unsuspected truths of their own linguistic concepts. Any first-year Latin student will, for instance, quickly encounter the unusual masculine nouns of the first declension, such as “nauta,” “poeta,” and “agricola.” What does it suggest about the realities of sailing and writing poetry and farming that these nouns, while masculine, take the feminine ending? Perhaps the student begins to sense that while these are three grueling activities, masculine indeed, they nonetheless possess a character of profound receptivity: the sailor forever at the ocean’s mercy; the poet listening, listening, for a snatch of inspired song; the farmer depending on sun and wind and rain for the fulfillment of his labor. 

While such quirks are present in any language, Latin deserves some privileges in that it gives students firsthand access to the very large portion of the Western tradition, which was first set down in Latin from Vergil and Ovid to Seneca and Cato to Augustine and Aquinas. If this is the tradition we seek to transmit, we would be remiss as educators not to hand down the very medium of transmission and to see that as many students as possible have the means to receive our great luminaries in their own words. 

In short, the study of Latin, which is itself often prefatory to the study of Greek (that little “treat,” as Churchill remarked) or of modern romance languages, is in many ways a lost key to coming to know the world we occupy. Its capacity to give students the world anew, stripped of the familiarity of all the usual words, and at the same time to reveal to students the space between words and things, is a tremendous power waiting to be taken up afresh by Catholic educators.

More Truly and More Strange: Scripture and the Vulgate

Catholics, as everyone knows, know next to nothing of the Bible. Yes, we have our Hahns; we have our Bergsmas. We have our Pitres and Barrons and Cavinses and Frs. Mike. Indeed, it’s just possible that, absent the last five centuries of scriptura vs. traditio, the accusation concerning our biblical illiteracy would never have been leveled. And yet (as Fr. Mike says), it is perhaps to be wondered whether the Bible plays as vivid a role in Catholic education as we might hope. For many of us who have grown familiar with the Scriptures, there is the danger that always attends familiarity—that of inattention, not to say contempt. It is just possible that, having heard the Sermon on the Mount fifty times before, I might be tempted to daydream through the fifty-first. It may transpire that the words of Genesis and Isaiah and Revelation fade into a spiritual miasma that only faintly animates the ear or the heart. 

If the Bible has become familiar in this manner, and if we seek especially to revive a love of Christ in the Scriptures in our educational institutions, we might again find help in Latin. The Vulgate, easily obtained, presents the familiar under the guise of the fresh, the ancient as hitherto unexplored. For the Latin student, the experience can be especially gratifying. For if the particular words of the Vulgate are new qua reading material, the concepts they convey are nevertheless quite familiar. If “in principio creavit Deus caelum et terram” is new to me, still, assuming even the faintest acquaintance with Scripture, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” is not. Thus, the familiar words made strange by the veil of Latin, and the veil of Latin words made familiar by the familiarity of the verses, the Vulgate can become both a highly effective pedagogical tool and a double-edged sword, piercing the soul anew for the reception of the Word.

They Divide the World Between Them

T. S. Eliot wrote that “Dante and Shakespeare divide the modern world between them; there is no third.” What the two giants would have made of such a sentiment seems fairly clear. Dante, who placed himself among the six greatest poets near the outset of his Inferno, would no doubt have spurned the Swan of Avon’s right to soar with him into the celestial aevum. And Shakespeare, who seems not to have cared at all about reputation or legacy or anything other than writing well and retiring early, would no doubt have shrugged and asked, “Who’s T. S. Eliot?”

Order Your Set Today

In any case, these two are without exception the great poets of the Christian era, and their study, especially in the case of Shakespeare, has for a long time played a critical role in education. If, in the English-speaking world, Dante’s Comedy is not very closely known, his name is at least associated with the Inferno. But hardly a student anywhere in the world can be produced who does not recognize Hamlet’s famous inquiry: “To be or not to be.” The names of Romeo and Juliet spring readily to any romantic lips. Julius Caesar is forever asking, “Et tu, Brute?” And, though they be not actively associated with Shakespeare in many people’s minds, countless sayings, phrases, and even words have come to populate our language and our cultural mindset thanks to the Bard. He appears to us everywhere, if not quite like the ghost of Hamlet’s father, then at least like a friendly spirit sent to haunt us from our linguistic complacence. 

For our purposes, these two poets are of the utmost importance because representing, as they do, the pinnacle of Christian poetry—particularly poetry written in the vernacular—their education would have been conducted in Latin and, in Shakespeare’s case especially, would have lain in little other than Latin. Thus, if we seek reasons to center education on the study of Latin once again, we need look no further than to the careers of these two men.

Dante entered history in the year 1265, at the height of the High Middle Ages, on the cusp of the Italian Renaissance. A student of one of St. Thomas Aquinas’s students, he was intimately familiar with the scholastic tradition as well as with the classical tradition. Indeed, if St. Augustine went so far as to model much of his Confessions on the Aeneid, then Dante, himself in many ways Augustinian, did him one better and, not content to make his literary avatar a pilgrim in the Vergilian vein, introduced Vergil himself as Dante’s guide through the Inferno, up the slopes of Purgatorio and to the guiding eyes of Beatrice. As Augustine points out, Christians have from the beginning possessed the rights of Israel to the Egyptian spoils where classical learning is concerned. Yet the reading of Vergil and Ovid can indeed present dangers to the learner who has not availed himself of Scripture and the Church’s magisterium, so much of which has been worked out in the Latin writings of the Church Fathers and the Scholastics. Dante’s vision, and the one which we ought to inculcate in our students, is one that sees the classical through the eyes of the Christian, taking what is good in the old and elevating it through the new wine of revelation. 

On the other hand, Shakespeare’s education was not so extensive as Dante’s. His formal schooling ended when he was around fifteen. In the boys’ schools of the Bard’s day, it was customary for students to learn Latin, to read a great deal of Latin, and to become well versed in all of the rhetorical devices the classical authors put to such extensive use. Indeed, from the ages of about seven to fifteen, they did little else between the hours of six in the morning and five in the evening but study Latin, with breaks for discipline, in which the masters were well schooled. If Shakespeare’s speakers can be taken as representative of his thought, “creeping like snail / Unwillingly to school,” his experience was not the most enjoyable. But it was, as Bill Bryson puts it, a magnificent way to learn “every possible rhetorical device and ploy.” And the evidence of this education is apparent in practically every line of Shakespeare’s poetry. Many of his plots, of course, are themselves drawn from the ancient world, and his endless experimentation with words themselves and of the seemingly infinite rhetorical modulations they allow both remind the reader of the great joy, the astonishing pleasure, of language and so keenly reflect the reality the reader has experienced that he can hardly help finding in Shakespeare’s plays the certification of his own experience. 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

That certification can always be found in the best of writing. The reader sees himself on the page in a way analogous to that in which Adam saw himself in Eve. He is handed back to himself via the gaze of the other. Understood in this way, Latin appears as a means for making its students more capable of being agents of grace in the world, revealing to their fellows the world around them, and so revealing them the more clearly to themselves. 

By learning faithfully to use our words, by tuning them to the highest pitch we can manage, we advance toward harmony with the Word himself. The study of Latin was critical to forming that capacity in the greatest of the Christian tradition’s poets; we set that study aside at our risk.

There are, of course, dangers to language. So often, words veil the things of the world in overfamiliarity so that words and things alike become so many contemptible sparrows, flitting about in the hedgerows of being. Then again, the magic of words can distract us from the reality of things, tempting us into worlds of our own verbal coinage. 

Nonetheless, words are a gift of the Word, and their proper use is key to our being made one with him. 

In canto XIV of his Paradiso, Dante writes, as he is brought to a higher heavenly sphere, “I saw myself translated.” The use of the metaphor reminds us that language is itself metaphorical in character, that it not only bears across meaning from one language-user to another but also has the capacity to bear us over from ourselves into the Word. Allowing our students to become well-versed in the language in which their tradition has been handed down is critical to helping them eventually to be translated into him.

items.title: Wednesday, August 12, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus is instructing his community in the difficult task of correcting an errant brother or sister.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ezekiel 9:1-7; 10:18-22

Then he cried in my hearing with a loud voice, saying, “Draw near, you executioners of the city, each with his destroying weapon in his hand.”And six men came from the direction of the upper gate, which faces north, each with his weapon for slaughter in his hand; among them was a man clothed in linen, with a writing case at his side. They went in and stood beside the bronze altar.

Now the glory of the God of Israel had gone up from the cherub on which it rested to the threshold of the house. The Lord called to the man clothed in linen, who had the writing case at his side; and said to him, “Go through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it.” To the others he said in my hearing, “Pass through the city after him, and kill; your eye shall not spare, and you shall show no pity. Cut down old men, young men and young women, little children and women, but touch no one who has the mark. And begin at my sanctuary.” So they began with the elders who were in front of the house. 7 Then he said to them, “Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain. Go!” So they went out and killed in the city.

Then the glory of the Lord went out from the threshold of the house and stopped above the cherubim. The cherubim lifted up their wings and rose up from the earth in my sight as they went out with the wheels beside them. They stopped at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the Lord; and the glory of the God of Israel was above them.

These were the living creatures that I saw underneath the God of Israel by the river Chebar; and I knew that they were cherubim. Each had four faces, each four wings, and underneath their wings something like human hands. As for what their faces were like, they were the same faces whose appearance I had seen by the river Chebar. Each one moved straight ahead.

Psalm
Psalm 113:1-2, 3-4, 5-6

Praise the Lord!
Praise, O servants of the Lord;
    praise the name of the Lord.
Blessed be the name of the Lord
    from this time on and forevermore.
From the rising of the sun to its setting
    the name of the Lord is to be praised.
The Lord is high above all nations,
    and his glory above the heavens.
Who is like the Lord our God,
    who is seated on high,
who looks far down
    on the heavens and the earth?

Gospel Reading
Matthew 18:15-20

“If another member of the church sins against you, go and point out the fault when the two of you are alone. If the member listens to you, you have regained that one. But if you are not listened to, take one or two others along with you, so that every word may be confirmed by the evidence of two or three witnesses. If the member refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church; and if the offender refuses to listen even to the church, let such a one be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. Again, truly I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about anything you ask, it will be done for you by my Father in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them.”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus is instructing his community in the difficult task of correcting an errant brother or sister. He tells them to avoid the practice of gossiping and complaining to others about a grievance; rather, they should confront the person who has offended them directly and courageously. That way, the difficulty is addressed, the loving concern of the complainant is evident, and the process of rumor, attack, counterattack, innuendo, and scapegoating is arrested.

Now, if the person does not respond to this loving intervention, “take one or two others along with you, so that every fact may be established on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” Thus, the wider community is involved, but only minimally—enough to bring the offender to repentance. Only if this small circle of the Church is ignored should one bring the complaint to the whole community.

What is so rich here is the pursuit of the issue (since speaking the truth, even when it is dangerous, is essential) coupled with a deep care for the person in question and also for the entire family of the Church (since love is our constant call).
